messages.author: 17d9c7a6e1a581b8
messages.subject: C++ API design
parts:
Hi everyone,

As I've been trying to figure out how PyStan can use, for example, the split
rhat and ess facilities from Stan, this caught my attention, it's a recent talk
from cppcon 2014 about the "Hourglass" pattern for interfacing between a C++
library and C/C++ "client" software. It does advocate header-only design but
there are some additional details that look interesting, including the
recommendation that points of contact be limited to C89 + const.

http://www.slideshare.net/StefanusDuToit/cpp-con-2014-hourglass-interfaces-for-c-apis

This seems like a good idea from my perspective!

Best,

-a

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] C++ API design
parts:
Going straight to C seems like a step backward to me. The C
type systems' much more impoverished, no exceptions, and it
introduces all the headaches of memory management.

I looked through the presentation and don't see how they
went from their goals to the "hourglass" design (to summarize,
C++ on both sides, narrowing down to C in the middle). The
"why does this help?" page seems mostly like a non-sequitur.
You hide the C++ data types but then have to introduce a whole
new parallel layer of C data types!

Are there specific problems with C++ you're having?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] C++ API design
parts:
I'm sympathetic to the idea that wrapping C++ is a hurdle and wrapping C is
easier. It's certainly the case for Python and I suspect it's true for other
languages.

I'm not having trouble per se -- it's more that there are too many choices. Does
one use a double *, a vector<double>, or an VectorXd, etc. Or does one allow all
three, and write three different functions for each function that accepts data
from the client? vector<double> seems like it has problems, like that it doesn't
allow mapping of existing memory (VectorXd doesn't have this problem). But if
one standardizes on VectorXd then one has to ask everyone to wrap Eigen too.

Best,

-a

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] C++ API design
parts:
On Sep 12, 2014, at 10:08 PM, Allen Riddell <a...@ariddell.org> wrote:

> I'm sympathetic to the idea that wrapping C++ is a hurdle and wrapping C is
> easier. It's certainly the case for Python and I suspect it's true for other
> languages.

I'm not sure about that. I think C++ is easier
for R through RStan, and of course it's no problem for
CmdStan, which is itself written in C++.

Is Python's interface mechanism just C so you're having
to wrap all the C++ in some kind of C interface before
Python can see it?

> I'm not having trouble per se -- it's more that there are too many choices. Does
> one use a double *, a vector<double>, or an VectorXd, etc. Or does one allow all
> three, and write three different functions for each function that accepts data
> from the client?

Are you talking about writing code that's part of PyStan?
I wouldn't think any of them would be visible to the
end user.

Don't you just need to convert whatever data
types Python uses to whatever data types Stan uses?

I think the way Michael and Daniel are moving the command-related
code to serve as a foundation for CmdStan/PyStan/Rstan, there will be
an Eigen-centric library in two namespaces, stan::services to do things
like call samplers or optimizers, and then a stan::interface for the
data-type conversion code, most likely formulated in terms of callbacks.

So I think any C interface would then wrap that interface.

As to callbacks, that'd mean function pointers specified from C that
then got wrapped up for C++ use (which isn't that hard if the C++
templates are general enough and expect functor arguments).

> vector<double> seems like it has problems, like that it doesn't
> allow mapping of existing memory (VectorXd doesn't have this problem).

Correct. I think that's one of the advantages for VectorXd.
And it makes MatrixXd contiguous too, whereas there are
lots of issues with vector<vector<double>> for locality.

> But if
> one standardizes on VectorXd then one has to ask everyone to wrap Eigen too.

Who is everyone here? You mean the developers of PyStan,
RStan, and CmdStan? Don't you already need Eigen wrapped up
for use with Stan already?

- Bob

I should have said I'm thinking beyond RStan and PyStan. What about, for
example, Julia, Ruby, and Rust?

I think in the not-long term, it would be better to make stanc produce a C++ file that is compatible with swig

http://www.swig.org/

which would allow basic usage with almost any scripting language (although not Julia, yet). This would just entail augmenting stanc to put something like

#ifdef SWIG
// declare functions to expose
#endif

into the C++ file.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] C++ API design
parts:
Someone brought up SWIG at the MSR open machine learning workshop.
It looks complicated. And there appear to be some issues with
R I didn't understand that are flagged in its doc. But the Shogun
people said they had good luck with it (though also noted it was
a pain in the ass to understand the first time around).

With the current RStan/PyStan, the model itself is only part of the
interface battle. The rest is all the sampling and optimization and
diagnosis and post-processing functions.

One possibility I've been playing with would be to use something
like SWIG to wrap the model, then provide a lightweight wrapper around
the CmdStan process for the rest of the interface. But that's
a different discussion, I think, that would make the interface at the
OS/process and file level, not at the C++ level.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] C++ API design
parts:
What complication there is with SWIG would mostly be downstream from us. I think all we have to do is add an #ifdef SWIG clause to the C++ file, and then someone who knows how to use SWIG should be able to take it from there (particularly if they can shell call bin/print from inside their scripting language). Also, if we get the cmake transition going again, we could probably provide a SWIG-based target.

Ben
